item.title: Doge overstated claims to have saved Americans $110bn, watchdog finds
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvg0rg9wmvlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Doge overstated claims to have saved Americans $110bn, watchdog finds - Published Some estimates made by Doge, the body charged with reducing US government spending, that it saved billions of dollars are "incorrect or lack supporting evidence", a watchdog has found. A report released on Thursday by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) has given an extensive review of Doge's claims about its so-called "Wall of Receipts", which reported savings of $110bn (£82bn) across contracts, grants and leases. "Several issues limit the transparency and reliability of these reported savings," the report stated. Asked for comment, a White House official said the administration told the GAO that all employees had to complete ethics training and follow financial disclosure requirements. Doge, the Department of Government Efficiency, was not an official government department. It launched at the start of President Trump's second term but closed last month. Its Wall of Receipts was a way of showing its purported savings in taxpayer money online. Elon Musk, the billionaire boss of Tesla and SpaceX who formerly led Doge but left in May 2025, initially promised to save as much as $2tn a year by slashing federal jobs and shuttering government programmes, among other cost-cutting measures. Even by Doge's own estimates, it fell short of that goal, as its website claims to have saved an estimated $214bn. "While Doge provided some information about estimated savings, several issues limit the transparency and reliability of these reported savings," the GAO report stated. It said Doge had not been transparent regarding the methods it used to calculate savings, highlighting it "did not provide sufficient information to verify the method used to calculate 96% of Doge-reported savings". Among its specific findings was that 108 of the 264 leases identified by Doge for termination were already in the process of ending before the body was established. That accounts for about $15.3m of the total $53.5m in savings Doge claimed. "The Wall of Receipts does not include an explanation of how the savings from terminated leases were calculated," the GAO said. Claims were also made about savings that were not achieved, like $1.7bn for ending a defence department contract for IT services. However, the contract was never terminated and thus no savings were achieved, according to the congressional watchdog's report. "While the Wall of Receipts includes some information about the data and sources underlying reported savings, it does not sufficiently disclose limitations affecting data quality," it assessed. The GAO audit, which was carried out at the request of Democratic Senators Gary Peters and Richard Blumenthal, covered savings data reported from 20 January 2025 through 7 July 2026. "Everyone supports rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government, but Doge was a slapdash and deceptive effort that misled the American people while doing real damage to the government's ability to serve them," Senator Peters said in a statement on Thursday. Under Musk, Doge pushed for massive reductions in the federal workforce, as well as the shuttering of programmes and even agencies such as the US Agency for International Development (USAID). Some of Doge's moves were met with legal fights, or were reversed. When the group's cost-cutting resulted in bird flu officials at the US Department of Agriculture being fired, the Trump administration looked to re-hire them days later. In a social media post last month announcing its closure, Doge said: "While the formal mission of Doge has come to an end, the mission to eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse will continue. Good stewardship of taxpayer dollars and accountable government are not temporary initiatives." Related topics - Published30 May 2025 - Published10 December 2025

item.title: German airport drone-bomb: Could Russia be involved?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgdmrxxkdxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
German airport drone-bomb: Could Russia be involved? - Published As Germany investigates how a drone loaded with explosives reached a runway at Leipzig airport, there is renewed talk in Europe of hybrid war. The interior minister is warning of a "new level of danger" from an attack that "may involve foreign powers". There is no proof at this stage to link the flying bomb directly to Russia, which denies any role. But as well as the means and the motive, Moscow does have form. The BBC has seen details of the investigation into a plot in 2024 in which Russian-linked proxies in Poland and Lithuania not only handled drones and explosives but also delivered them to Germany. The flying bomb The quadcopter was discovered at Leipzig airport late on Tuesday night, forcing one runway into lockdown as a bomb disposal robot rolled into action. On the tarmac close by were several Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes, stripes along their enormous bodies in the blue and yellow of the country's flag. One reads, "Be Brave Like Kherson", the southern city now on the frontline of Russia's invasion. Pictures published by German media suggest the drone was a relatively small device which airport staff spotted "floating" between the Ukrainian planes. Around the same time, a DHL cargo plane collided with an "unidentified object" as it pulled up into the sky, unable to land in Leipzig. Teams are still working to establish whether that was a second drone. They are also trying to trace who launched the devices and why. A previous plot A previous Russian-backed plot involving Leipzig airport could provide clues. In 2024, a parcel containing a sophisticated incendiary device caught fire at the airport's DHL hub shortly before it was loaded onto a plane. Similar packages then ignited in the UK and Poland, causing extensive damage. A group of men are currently on trial in both Lithuania and Poland, where prosecutors believe they were part of a substantial network of proxies recruited by Russian military intelligence. But there was a subplot that has been little discussed before. Last September, Lithuanian prosecutors said that investigators had also seized RDX explosives meant for "other terrorist attacks". The amount was significant: equivalent to 6kg of TNT. "Some of the devices were manufactured to intensify the blast," the prosecutor added. The BBC has since had access to case documents that describe how several of the men on trial were paid to transport those explosives around Europe, concealed in cans of sweetcorn and chopped tomatoes. The detonators were hidden inside headphone sets. The suspects also handled drone parts and the case talks specifically of attachments, suitable for holding a bomb. Prosecutors allege that some of the items were brought into the EU from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Almost two dozen suspects have been charged with terror offences, but with the men's handlers still at large, believed to be in Russia, it is not clear whether the entire network was disbanded or all the hidden material found. While there is no evidence of a link to the Leipzig drone bomb, the 2024 plot certainly highlights the potential. Vladyslav's story One of the suspects charged in Poland, a Ukrainian called Vladyslav D., described in detail to investigators how he made multiple long car trips in July 2024 following instructions from someone he knew as "Warrior". He has since pleaded not guilty in court. One message sent him to the edge of a Lithuanian forest where he found a carrier bag containing "three or four packs of headphones", soggy with rain. He had already collected two cans of corn "lightly covered with soil" from another location, telling investigators he had no idea what was inside. He was ordered to leave the headphones many hours' drive away in Poland where he noticed "a guy on a bicycle" collect them from beside the road. For another assignment he received a pin for a location inside a Lithuanian cemetery and was told to dig beneath some plastic flowers. He quickly uncovered a bin bag wrapped in brown tape. "Inside were drone components: small plastic propellers, I think four pieces," Vladyslav told investigators. These items were to be left by a road in central Poland for pick-up. Finally there was a trip to Germany where he was given the code to access a hostel room in Dusseldorf. He was instructed to leave the drones and other items inside. The intended targets were never revealed. Moscow's motive? In statements to investigators, Vladyslav D. said he was paid more than $2,000 (£1,487) in cryptocurrency for his efforts. His motive was clear. And what about the Leipzig case? Few details about the drone bomb are yet public. Some German sources report that the explosive was Semtex, which contains RDX - the explosive found in the food cans in a Lithuanian cemetery. We do not know how much the drone found at the airport was carrying and the physical damage may have been limited. "The drone casing, if it was metal, might have put a hole in the plane but just a blast wave probably would just have dented it unless they put some fragmentation inside," explosives expert Professor Jackie Akhavan of Cranfield University explained. But if Russia was behind this, its aim was more likely to sow fear. Andrei Soldatov, an expert on Russia's intelligence agencies, said it "makes sense" to suspect Moscow, pointing to a clear pattern of sabotage and hostile activity, from arson attacks on facilities supporting Ukraine to drones over sensitive sites in Europe. Germany is one of Kyiv's biggest suppliers of military aid. "It's a message. You get something like that [bomb] into one of the biggest European airports and you send the message that, 'Guys, we can do that. Remember'," Soldatov explained. "You hint to the adversary that you might cause a really big problem: that tomorrow might be more serious." And the potential motive? Moscow is under intense pressure from Ukraine's long-scale drone attacks, he said, and the fact that Russian President Vladimir Putin "has been humiliated, repeatedly". International response "We are aware of the incident, which the German authorities continue to investigate," a Nato official told the BBC. Antonov Airlines has also been cautious so far in its response. The firm supplies planes for certain Nato operations but declined to say whether that includes military support for Ukraine. Asked whether the Ukrainian planes might have been targeted, a spokeswoman in Kyiv told the BBC: "We are not making any such assumptions…We don't know what this drone was or why it was there." But Russia watchers are clear. "This is Russian interference," said John Lough of the New Eurasian Strategies (NEST) Centre. "It's all part of undermining support for Ukraine by pointing to the dangers of escalation and, frankly, scaring the German authorities." He sees high potential for a surge in such hybrid attacks now because Ukraine has "changed the balance" of the war. "My expectation is that such activity will increase quite sharply over the coming months. I think it's a dangerous moment." Related topics - Published1 day ago - Published1 day ago

item.title: Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr7kldz4djno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity - Published Warning: This story contains details some may find distressing A 17-year-old Sudanese girl holds a young child in her arms with a heavy calm that belies her age and the concerns she has for his future. "This son of mine has no father, no birth certificate and no national number," Amira, whose name has been changed to protect her identity, tells the BBC. Looking down at him, she speaks slowly as if still trying to grasp the details of what has happened to her since the civil war erupted in Sudan. She and her family used to live in the eastern neighbourhoods of el-Fasher, a city that came under siege from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been in a brutal power struggle with the military since April 2023. El-Fasher was the army's last stronghold in the western region of Darfur until it fell to the RSF and allied Arab militias after 18 months last October. For the tens of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city, it was a nightmare – with constant bombardment, clashes and suffering from a lack of food. In the end Amira and her family decided to flee early in 2025, desperate to find a safer area. But as they snuck out on a road south-west of the city, she says she was abducted by three armed men from the RSF and held captive. "They blindfolded me and took me to the Tabit area south of el-Fasher. I was locked in a room for two months, and every day one of them raped me in turn," she recounts in a low voice After weeks in captivity, she discovered she was pregnant and became very sick. Amira says when the men wanted to get rid of her, they dropped her near the area she had been captured. It was with the help of other people fleeing el-Fasher that she was taken to receive medical help. Months later, at a humanitarian hub that was not under RSF control, she gave birth at a hospital run by the International Medical Corps. There she received some support from a Sudanese aid organisation - the Nada Al-Azhar Foundation for Disaster Prevention and Sustainable Development (Nada). The group was also able to find her family, who had made it to a camp where hundreds of thousands of people from el-Fasher have sought refuge. It was a huge relief for them all to be reunited, but the family still face challenges - one being that eight months after giving birth, Amira has been unable to register her son's birth. "Even getting a birth notification from the hospital requires information that doesn't exist," says Amira, explaining that she is unable to provide any details about the child's father. Without this she cannot organise any official recognition of the baby's legal identity. "I can't get him vaccinated, or enrol him in nursery or school," she says. "I'm afraid for his future because he isn't registered at all. My economic situation is very difficult, and I can't afford his treatment or care. I can't even go to work for fear of being exposed to violence again." According to Nada, Amira's story is not an isolated case, but part of a reality repeated in areas experiencing conflict across Sudan. This is because many children are being born in complex circumstances, often without the knowledge of the father - meaning their births cannot be registered, explains Abu Bakr Yousif Yaqoub, Nada's director of protection programmes. "Registering a child requires identity information, a national number and a birth certificate. But when the father is absent or unknown, it becomes extremely difficult," he tells the BBC from el-Fasher. "The mother is often alone, and sometimes she herself is still a child who needs care, which limits her ability to care for her baby. "There are also health challenges related to the lack of follow-up on essential vaccinations, which begin at birth and continue through the child's early years." He warns that this situation does not just affect a child's early years but extends to their future education and as an adult being able to travel or obtain official documents. It is not easy to obtain data about the number of children that have been born as a result of rape in Sudan. According to Nada's director general, Shaza Ahmed, this comes down to social stigma as the true numbers are not recorded. "Women who experience such assaults do not feel comfortable reporting them," she tells the BBC, speaking from Port Sudan, an army-held city in the east of Sudan. "Unfortunately, most of the mothers of these children are themselves children - girls under the age of 18. Therefore, they cannot make the decision to go officially to court or the police, as they need a guardian to accompany them." She notes that 90% of the cases recorded by her organisation involve families refusing to allow official reporting of the sexual assaults that led to pregnancy. "As a Sudanese woman, my greatest fear and concern for children born as a result of rape is that we are facing a whole generation that will live under stigma, danger and fear," Ahmed says. "These children will not receive respect from society, their well-being will not be truly protected, and above all, they will not have access to services or their rights." For Ahmed they are not being treated as if they are "fully human", even though Sudanese law does grant all children the right to obtain an identity. Sudanese lawyer Majida Idris explains that the Child Act of 2010 allows for the registration of children born outside marriage. But it relies on the mother being willing to file a report that she has been assaulted - because this kick starts the registration process. Once reported, the case is then referred to social services for documentation, before being sent to the civil registry, where the child is registered under the mother's name and given a full legal name according to procedures. However, Idris says that the reality during war is completely different, especially in Darfur, where the ongoing conflict has led to the collapse of civil services and the shutdown of civil registry offices, leaving thousands of children unregistered. "The absence of documents does not just mean the absence of a piece of paper - it means denying the child access to education, healthcare and legal recognition," she tells the BBC. The lawyer says it is imperative to reactivate civil registry offices in accessible areas and intensify legal efforts to ensure children obtain their right to identity and legal recognition. Amira and her child remain in Darfur - and therefore in administrative limbo. Her mother admits that the lack of paperwork for her grandson is a worry. Yet for the moment the family is overwhelmed with gratitude to have found one another again. Amira has also been offered emotional and psychological support sessions and other advice by Nada - which is a comfort to the family. "I was so extremely worried until I found her. I hadn't been eating or drinking," Amira's mother told the BBC. "The reunion was like a miracle from God. To see our daughter back sitting among us is a gift and blessing that could not be thanked enough for." item.title: 'Put your phone down': K-pop band weighs in on concert etiquette
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39ep3p0ld1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'Put your phone down': K-pop band weighs in on concert etiquette - Published Kicking off their global tour in the South Korean city of Incheon, the five members of K-pop boy band Cortis saunter onto stage in casual, streetwear-inspired outfits, exuding an effortlessly cool vibe. "Put your phone down," one of the members bellows. Piercing screams erupt. A sea of illuminated screens flickers back. "I told you, put your phone down," he repeats, louder this time. Some fans do just that, but the packed stadium vibrates harder with cheers as thousands of phones stay in the air. It's hard to say how serious this theatrical command is. "Put your phone down" is also the name of Cortis's ongoing concert tour, which started in Incheon on 18 July and will head to cities like New York and Los Angeles before returning to Seoul later this month. The refrain reflects a message the band has long pushed: that fans should stop watching concerts through six-inch screens and engage with their performances in real life. It's drawn mixed reactions from their fandom: fan-filmed content is a valuable social currency in K-pop. Park Ji-yeon, for one, could not bring herself to stop recording Cortis's performances. The 22-year-old had specially rented a new, top-tier smartphone for both days of the Cortis concert just so she could film in the highest quality. "I was standing right at the front, and I couldn't bring myself to put my phone down because I don't know if I'll ever get this opportunity again," she tells the BBC. "I usually film concerts because I know a lot of those memories will fade as soon as I leave the venue." While fans like Park continued to film, some heeded the band's call. Kim Ga-eun, 25, who was seated in the amphitheatre-style venue, saw it all. "People in the back of the standing section were having a great time dancing together. I thought that really reflected the intention behind the concert," she says. Cortis has had a whirlwind year since debuting last year under record label BigHit Music - part of the company that created pop sensation BTS. Most of its members are teenagers. The oldest of the group, James, is just 20 years old. Their music videos have each amassed millions of views. Over the weekend they performed at Lollapalooza, the famed music festival in Chicago. The band's name, Cortis, is derived from the phrase "colour outside the lines", which according to their record label is meant to encapsulate the band's free spirit and refusal to conform to societal rules - which, in this case, appears to include telling fans to resist the temptation of the phone camera. They join a prominent wave of artists around the world who have been advocating the same. Singers like Phoebe Bridgers and Alicia Keys have required their concert attendees to use lock pouches - sealed bags that allow people to hold on to their phones without being able to access them. Few have gone as far as British rock group Suede, whose frontman Brett Anderson leapt over a barricade during a 2023 performance in Singapore to grab at fans' phones. Billie Eilish, who has defended filming as a way for fans to relive precious memories after a show, gently cooed to her front row audience during a performance in Amsterdam: "Put your phone down, I'm right here." Even BTS, K-pop's golden boys, have made similar requests. "Stop looking at your phone screen. Just look at me," BTS member Jungkook teased the audience at one concert. "From the artists' perspective, interacting with fans is a really important part of performing, so I think they want people to focus more on that than on their phones," Park says of Cortis's anti-mobile rallying cry. After all, fancams - zoomed-in videos focusing on a single celebrity - are a prized currency in K-pop communities. Once shared online, people meticulously study the choreography in them and delight in catching subtle movements and expressions by their favourite band members. These clips live on as fodder for collective swooning and fan-made montages. And this is why Cortis's incessant calls to for people to put their phones down have rubbed some the wrong way - in a fan culture that's obsessed with capturing every moment. After the first day of their concert, disgruntled comments emerged online among fans. "I spent over one million won ($700; £520) attending both days," Park says, referring to the sum of not just concert tickets but also additional expenses like transport and accommodation. "I think a lot of fans spent similar amounts of money, so constantly hearing them asking us to put our phones down made some fans even more frustrated." These murmurs appear to have reached Cortis, who fans say dialled down their message on the second day of the concert. "On the first day, the message felt more like, 'Let's put our phones down and have fun together.' On the second day, it changed slightly to, 'We understand why you want to film, so let's just make sure we enjoy ourselves together,'" Kim recalls. "They said filming was okay, but they wanted us to enjoy the concert together, and that 'Put Your Phone Down' was more of a mindset."

item.title: India is a nation of walkers - but its cities forgot them
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3e4enkrqro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
India is a nation of walkers - but its cities forgot them - Published For much of my life, walking in Indian cities has felt less like exercising a right than negotiating an obstacle course. I grew up in Kolkata, where wide pavements disappeared beneath rows of hawkers. I moved to Delhi, where roads seemed designed almost exclusively for cars. Now I live in Gurugram, where footpaths vanish into rubble and garbage, are abruptly blocked by parked vehicles or construction, or sit uncomfortably high above the road. So when India's Supreme Court declared in June that the right to walk safely on designated footpaths was a fundamental right, external, it felt less like judicial activism than common sense arriving decades late. Walking is the most democratic form of transport. Yet it is also the one India's cities have neglected most consistently. It's remarkable because India remains, above all, a nation of walkers. Around 45 million people walk to work every day, according to census-based estimates, compared with only about 5.4 million who commute in private cars, jeeps or vans. Nearly a third of urban workers walk to work, while virtually every bus or metro journey begins and ends on foot. Add school runs, shopping trips and other everyday journeys, and walking dominates urban mobility. A 2019 survey of selected cities found that 63% of all journeys were made on foot, making pedestrians the single largest group of road users. Many are what researchers call "captive pedestrians" - people who walk not by choice but because they cannot afford another option. Women are especially dependent on walking. Yet the people who contribute least to congestion and pollution often face the greatest risks. The evidence is harrowing. Even where pavements exist, they are often broken, narrow or inaccessible to older people, children and those with disabilities. They are also blocked by motorcycles, swallowed by parked cars, encroachments or excavated for utility works. Faded zebra crossings are treated as little more than road markings no-one respects. Flyovers speed traffic while forcing pedestrians into hazardous detours below. A landmark 2011 study of six Indian cities found that India's streets routinely fail pedestrians because of "poor and unsafe" infrastructure. The Walkability in Indian Cities report by the Clean Air Initiative for Asian Cities (CAI-Asia) gave the surveyed cities a median walkability score of just 47 out of 100, with the worst conditions around public transport terminals - ironically the places where most journeys begin and end on foot As Geetam Tiwari, a transport scholar at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi puts it, pedestrians have been "pushed to the margins of the road networks" forcing them to "jostle for space with motor vehicles". The price is paid in lives. Officially pedestrians account for roughly a fifth of road deaths, external, but independent studies cited by Tiwari estimate the share is closer to 30-40%. Pedestrians are also the second-largest group of road accident victims after two-wheeler riders. In Delhi and Mumbai, they account for more than half of all road deaths. According to a World Bank study, crashes already cost India an estimated 3-5% of its GDP each year through lost productivity, healthcare costs and disability. The Supreme Court case arose from one such tragedy: a five-year-old boy crushed by a truck while walking to school with his father. The judges responded with unusual eloquence. Walking, Justice PS Narasimha wrote, is "the simplest of the simple human activity, inextricably connected to life". Roads therefore impose a corresponding duty on the state to provide safe footpaths. "The fundamental right to walk on demarcated footpaths shall override the privilege of a motorised vehicle," he declared. The judgment challenges decades of Indian urban planning, where progress has often been measured in kilometres of expressways, flyovers and elevated corridors. Streets were engineered to move vehicles as quickly as possible, while the one road user every citizen inevitably becomes - the pedestrian - largely disappeared from planners' imagination. "People know about the latest cars, but walking has become invisible," says Rishi Aggarwal, who has spent more than a decade trying to change that mindset in Mumbai. Through city walks and public talks, his advocacy group, Walking Project, encourages residents to notice what they have stopped seeing: broken pavements, blocked crossings and unsafe junctions - and compare them with the standards pedestrians are entitled to expect. "When people become apathetic, they stop observing the street," he says. In a city where an estimated 15 million walking trips are made every day, Aggarwal argues, it is not just footpaths that have disappeared from view, but also the millions of people who depend on them. For Rahul Goel, a transportation researcher at Delhi's Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), the problem begins with governance. "Are footpaths maintained and cleaned? Does the city ensure they aren't encroached upon?" he says. "In Delhi, many roads do have footpaths, but they're often unusable because of poor governance." Poor design makes matters worse. Cars parked perpendicular to the kerb often conceal footpaths or block them altogether, while vehicles parked directly on pavements are a common sight. Footpaths are often too narrow for the number of pedestrians. Many are so high above the road that older people, wheelchair users and others with limited mobility struggle to use them. Others end abruptly, forcing people back onto the carriageway. "If the footpath is discontinuous, it's simply more convenient to keep walking on the road," says Goel. He believes the deeper problem is one of priorities. "Urban transport governance is still centred on moving vehicles. Reducing congestion and maximising road space for motor traffic take precedence over pedestrians," he says. Civic agencies are often reluctant to widen footpaths because they view carriageway space as sacrosanct. That mindset, Goel argues, is reinforced by public pressure. Traffic jams dominate headlines and social media, pushing authorities to keep vehicles moving. In Delhi, many mid-block crossings have been replaced by U-turns to reduce stoppages, forcing pedestrians onto foot overbridges. "People don't just need to walk along a road," says Goel. "They need to be able to cross it safely too." The result is a stark urban inequality. In Gurugram, a high-speed arterial road cuts through busy neighbourhoods with few safe crossings. Domestic workers, labourers and other pedestrians routinely dodge speeding traffic, and many are killed trying to cross. Only after the death toll mounted did authorities begin building footbridges. Across India's cities, those who cannot afford cars or motorcycles are left to risk their lives on roads that barely accommodate pedestrians. Those who can drive claim an ever-larger share of public space, while walking becomes a leisure activity confined to gated communities, parks or gym treadmills. In a country grappling with rising obesity and lifestyle diseases, cities have turned the most basic form of exercise into something not just inconvenient, but too often dangerous. Clearly, making people walk will require far more than a court order. "Walking as a fundamental right should lead to pedestrian-friendly cities, not just pedestrian-friendly streets," says Tiwari. That means rethinking how cities are designed. Some countries have adopted default urban speed limits of 30km/h or 20mph to protect pedestrians, regardless of the type of road. Achieving that, Tiwari says, requires redesigning streets by narrowing traffic lanes, altering road surfaces and introducing other traffic-calming measures. The judges also reflected on walking as something far greater than a way of getting from one place to another. It can be "necessity for the poor, meditation for some, an act of resistance for others and a path to discovery. Walking, they noted, also helped shape India's freedom struggle". As writer Sumana Roy notes, external, India's political history has often unfolded on foot -from Gandhi's "salt march" to Dandi to Subhas Chandra Bose's "Delhi Chalo" (March to Delhi) and the many protest marches that followed. For Tiwari, that broader understanding of walking should also shape how cities are built. "Walking is more than a travel option," she says. "Therefore a safe walking infrastructure requires more than creating footpaths and safe crossing. Walking spaces have to integrate activities like spaces of street vendors, shaded paths, areas for resting for old people and sometimes space where children can play." For decades, Indian cities have asked how to move more vehicles. The top court has reminded them to ask a simpler one: how do people walk? I'd settle for something wonderfully unremarkable: a footpath that simply carries me from one end of the street to the other. - Published17 November 2024

item.title: Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78g3glpl8wo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president? - Published For now, beleaguered Fifa president Gianni Infantino still has some allies in world football, particularly in parts of the world where less well-off football associations have benefited from his presidency. Infantino's position has been under scrutiny since his controversial plan to sell stakes in Fifa's global competitions to private investors was scrapped having been opposed by some regional governing bodies. Late on Thursday, the executive committee of the African confederation (Caf) unanimously confirmed its support for Infantino, after leading African football administrators sent messages backing him. Five of the seven African countries on the Fifa Council - Egypt, Morocco, Niger, Mauritania and Comoros - have already supported him publicly. Support from the continent largely stems from Fifa's Forward programme, a funding scheme Infantino introduced in 2016 that many African federations have become increasingly reliant on to fund football projects in areas where commercial and government investment in the sport is limited. Our reporters and correspondents have explained below where some of Africa's key footballing nations stand. - Faisal Islam: Four reasons why Fifa's World Cup plan never stacked up - Published6 days ago Morocco Morocco's rise as one of Africa's football success stories has largely been driven by government funding, but the country has also become a key partner for Fifa. Morocco's capital, Rabat, is home to Fifa's Africa regional office, they have hosted Fifa Club World Cups, a women's U17 World Cup and will co-host the men's 2030 World Cup alongside Spain and Portugal. Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) president Fouzi Lekjaa reaffirmed his support for Infantino after he withdrew the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal last week. In a statement, Lekjaa described Infantino's decision to withdraw it as "wise", adding it put the unity of Fifa's 211 member associations first. Infantino also received the backing of senior football executives at a meeting in Morocco on Wednesday, following a turbulent period after the proposal's collapse. Reporting by Celestine Karoney Egypt Egypt is home to the Confederation of African Football headquarters and remains one of Infantino's strongest institutional allies in Africa. The relationship is reinforced by the influence of Hany Abo Rida, a Fifa Council member and one of the continent's most prominent football administrators, who has maintained close ties with Infantino since his election in 2016. During Infantino's presidency, Egypt has benefited from Fifa's Forward programme, which has funded infrastructure projects, youth development, coach education and women's football. Like other African member associations, the Egyptian Football Association has also received increased development funding under Fifa's expanded investment strategy, while new and expanded football competitions have created additional commercial and sporting opportunities. But support for Infantino in Egypt is accompanied by growing expectations. Officials and observers increasingly argue that Fifa's engagement with Africa should extend beyond financial assistance. Greater emphasis is being placed on good governance, transparency, sustainable football development and giving Cafmore room to shape the continent's own priorities. Reporting by Mohamed Alkaaoud in Cairo DR Congo The Congolese Football Federation (Fecofa) has welcomed Infantino's decision to withdraw the controversial Forward Enterprise proposal, calling it "wise" in a statement earlier this month. Pointing to a decade of work promoting football worldwide - and in particular his support of African nations - the federation stressed that the episode should not overshadow Infantino's wider record. Fecofa stressed that the episode, born of good intentions, should not overshadow Infantino's wider record. It pointed to his decade of work promoting football worldwide, and particularly his support for African federations and those with fewer resources. The federation said it had "greatly benefited" from Fifa's programmes, citing investment in development and infrastructure. The declaration was signed by Véron Mosengo‑Omba, elected president of Fecofa in May 2026. His election ended a period of uncertainty following the resignation of Constant Omari Selemani in 2021 and the subsequent Fifa‑appointed Normalisation Committee established in April 2023. Mosengo‑Omba assured Infantino of Fecofa's "full support" would continue beyond 2027, recalling mandates renewed in Paris in 2019 and Kigali in 2023. The statement underlines the Democratic Republic of Congo's alignment with Fifa leadership at a time when divisions remain sharp elsewhere in world football. Reporting by Emery Makumeno Nigeria The Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) has largely aligned itself towards a supportive stance for Infantino's leadership, despite the wider backlash globally. For a football federation facing chronic funding constraints and enormous infrastructure needs, Infantino's proposed plans would have been difficult to dismiss. Former president of the NFF and deputy chairman of Fifa's Men's National Teams Competitions Committee, Amaju Pinnick, argued that Infantino's plan would deliver a much-needed financial boost to every member association without over-relying on local governments. Nigeria is eligible for up to $8m (£5.95m), for the current Fifa Forward funding, despite failing to qualify for the last two men's World Cup tournaments. The most prominent Forward project currently under way in Nigeria is the redevelopment of the NFF Technical Centre in the capital, Abuja. The project, funded with approximately $4.88m, includes the reconstruction of training pitches, and the construction of a modern accommodation complex for Nigeria's national teams. Reporting by Emmanuel Akindubuwa What others in Africa have said The Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture of South Africa, Gayton McKenzie, posted on X saying that Infantino had been "very good to African football". "Africa should be cautious in joining the public lynching of Infantino. He has been very good to African football. "We can debate his ideas but let's not forget who has been a friend to us. Many of those calling for his head want the old status quo back too." Speaking to the BBC after Infantino's proposal emerged, football officials from Malawi and Uganda said Fifa investment had transformed the game both on and off the pitch, arguing such funding is vital given the financial realities facing many African nations. "Malawi needs money. Malawi needs stadiums, our government cannot manage to give us even $1m every year for football," Malawi FA president Fleetwood Haiya told BBC's Newsday programme. "Our government is not able to make sure that they have medical supplies in hospitals [and] at the same time to look at football," he said. President of the Gambia Football Federation, Lamin Kaba Bajo, told BBC Sport: "As far as I'm concerned, most of my colleagues are concerned, we'll encourage him [Infantino] to stay, and we'll do everything within our means to ensure that he is re-elected come next year, 2027. "That's my personal opinion as president of the federation, and a good number of African memberships also stand on that line. He is here to stay." But support for the project on the continent was not universal. Former Sierra Leone FA president and ex-Fifa Council member Isha Johansen was among African voices opposing it, warning it risked over-commercialising football asking, "What price does one have to pay in order to get to this elevated development for football in Africa?" Johansen urged African football chiefs to think carefully about the game's future. Last month, Caf president Patrice Motsepe lauded Infantino for his "excellent work" after this year's World Cup and hailed him as "a good friend". "He is loyal to Africa," Motsepe said on 22 July. "When people have been loyal to you, you never stab them in the back." Other nations are yet to comment publicly, including Senegal, whose men's team is the second-highest ranked African team behind Morocco.

item.title: Livestreamer's murder raises questions over relations between Mexico's creators and cartels
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckg9dwz8p30o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Livestreamer's murder raises questions over relations between Mexico's creators and cartels - Published The killing of a young influencer, caught on camera as he was livestreaming in Mexico's Sinaloa state, has raised questions about possible links between content creators and criminal cartels in this violence-wracked part of the country. On the stream, two men on a motorbike can be seen riding up to César Gastélum, who is chatting to two friends outside a fast food restaurant in the city of Culiacán. The murder happens within seconds: the driver of the bike shoots him in the head at close range before fleeing. While the Sinaloa state prosecutor's office provided little detail about the incident, it did say that its lines of investigations included a number of posts Gastélum had published, "some of which refer to a criminal group". Gastélum is not the first influencer to be murdered in Sinaloa. At least 10 content creators have been killed in the state since a deadly war broke out between two rival factions of the Sinaloa criminal cartel two years ago. Officials say Gastélum had not received any threats from criminal groups, nor was he under investigation by police for any alleged criminal links, as had been the case with some of the influencers targeted in the past. But according to Claudia Arruñada, a communications expert at Mexico's Iberoamerican University, the worlds of social media and the criminal underworld can sometimes become intertwined - with at times deadly consequences. "The [social media] algorithm and the narcos promote the same thing: consumption and luxury as ultimate values, to be achieved in the quickest way possible." "The model for success is no longer based on methodically working on your career, but rather on having a meteoric rise," she adds. Arruñada argues that in some cases influencers have promoted narcoculture, by showing luxurious lifestyles to their followers and linking these riches to the exploits of narcos. Gastélum often shared pictures of himself posing with expensive cars, enjoying the nightlife and going on luxury trips, as well as comedy clips and challenges. In one photo he posted, he could be seen at the grave of Leobardo Aispuro, better known as "El Gordo Peruci", an influencer who was murdered in 2024. Content creators like him have vehemently rejected being labelled as "narco-influencers", arguing that the sheer fact of being a young public figure showing off a luxury lifestyle can make you a target in Culiacán. Some studies suggest that the cartels - which function very much like multinational companies with various business interests - do use content creators as community managers, to promote their "brand". When rival factions turn on each other, those seen as spreading propaganda for one group can quickly become targets for its sworn enemies. This is what appears to have happened in January 2025, when leaflets were dropped from an aircraft onto the streets of Culiacán. The pamphlets accused 25 influencers and musicians of having links to "La Mayiza", a faction of the Sinaloa cartel involved in a deadly confrontation with rivals "Los Chapitos". Four of those named had already been killed and were marked on the leaflet as "eliminated". Two more have been murdered since. Gastélum's name was not on that list but his killing is nevertheless seen as the latest in a trend seeing influencers being targeted. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Wednesday that local and national authorities would go after those who had murdered him - and those who had ordered it. Her government is trying to sever the link between popular culture and the criminal underworld, denouncing narcocorridos, songs which glorify criminals, as well as tackling crime head on. Official figures suggest the number of murders fell by 48% in 2025. But there is little doubt that killings like that of Gastélum - witnessed by his followers who were online at the time as it unfolded - strengthen the impression that narcos continue to wield power - and death - not just on the streets of Culiacán but also on digital platforms. Update: The original image on this story was an agency photo which purported to show César Gastélum the influencer. However, it showed a musician of the same name which was wrongly labelled. We have replaced the photo. Related topics - Published2 days ago - Published16 May 2025

item.title: In Odesa, no-one is safe from Russia's new Black Sea strikes
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy8ev4y172yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
In Odesa, no-one is safe from Russia's new Black Sea strikes - Published "My crane operator, my partner, died five metres from me… The driver remained in the cabin. He also died." Svitlana Halchenko winces as she remembers the Russian ballistic missile which exploded at work in Odesa, killing her colleagues. Svitlana works as a warehouse shift manager at the city's main port. Despite her injuries – she walks with a limp, pieces of shrapnel still embedded in her leg and back – Svitlana is determined to keep working. But her normally bustling workplace is largely silent. Russia is ramping up its efforts to strangle Ukraine's commercial links to the outside world, launching attacks all along the country's Black Sea coastline. From damaged port infrastructure to listing ships with bridges blackened and containers still smouldering, the evidence is everywhere. Nowhere more so than out towards the horizon, where the approaches to Ukraine's once bustling ports – Odesa, Chornomorsk, Pivdennyi – are almost devoid of ships. Svitlana maintains a brave smile throughout our conversation, but her distress is painfully obvious. Her fingers constantly twist a tissue as she tries to maintain her composure and she gazes into the distance as tears well up behind her glasses. The last few weeks have been worse than ever. "It's been very difficult for morale," she says with a deep sigh. "A lot of sirens, a lot of shaheds [drones], a lot of hits. People are very tense." My crane operator, my partner, died five metres from me… The driver remained in the cabin. He also died According to Ukraine's port administration, July saw 57 Russian attacks on civilian vessels, 22 of them at sea, and a further 67 hits on port infrastructure. While there have been Russian attacks on international vessels before, they've never been so numerous or so deadly. On July 19, a Turkish-owned cargo vessel, Golden Leo, was struck by three Russian missiles, killing nine Indian and Syrian crew members and a Ukrainian pilot. The ship, carrying Ukrainian corn, sank off Odesa a week later. According to the global shipping journal Lloyd's List, the Black Sea may now be the most dangerous place for shipping in the world - with July the deadliest month for merchant seamen, external since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. At his union's offices in the port city, Oleg Grygoriuk, Chairman of the Marine Transport Workers Union of Ukraine, says his members are suffering. "There are a lot of veterans who already served their country," he says, "and they literally say that being in the port is more scary than being on the front line." Odesa's proximity to Russian-occupied territory means that workers often have little time to react. "A missile flies from Crimea within a minute," he says. "If you are sitting in a crane, you need three and a half minutes to get down and go to the shelter. There's literally no time to do that." On a rare visit to one of the area's main ports, we saw almost no sign of movement. Hundreds of metres of berths sat empty and towering gantry cranes stood idle as a skeleton crew conducted maintenance. The military authorities allowed the visit on strict condition that we neither name the facility nor film anything. Ukraine doesn't want Russia to know what has and hasn't been damaged or reveal details that might aid Moscow in further targeting. Two damaged cargo vessels were moored nearby. Both had suffered severe damage to the superstructure, where the bridge and crew quarters are located. Just one lone freighter was seen moving towards the port. "My heart is broken," a senior manager told us on condition we didn't name him. "Normally there's a queue, even out at sea, waiting for a berth." "There was a deal," he said, referring to the UN-brokered 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative, under which Russia agreed to lift its blockade on Ukraine's agricultural exports. The agreement established safe maritime corridors to Odesa's main ports. "They stopped the deal in the middle of 2023, but they didn't start attacking it until recently," the manager said. "Today they do it systematically." Halfway through our tour, sirens sounded, forcing us to seek shelter for several minutes as a Russian jet-powered drone flew overhead. Weary dock workers scanned their phones for updates until the all-clear sounded. The manager said recent alerts have forced the port to shut down for 15 out of 24 hours. Technically, the port is open, as are all the others in the area. There is no prohibition on commercial ships attempting to use them. But the risks are clearly too great for most shipowners. "There is barely anybody who wants to call because there is a huge problem with people getting killed," says Andrey Stavnitser, co-owner and CEO of one of the largest ports in the area. "We can see that the whole supply chain is on hold." Stavnitser says Russia is almost certainly retaliating for Ukraine's recent, highly successful attacks on Russian shipping, including sanctioned vessels carrying oil, as well as other ships involved in ferrying supplies to Russian-occupied Crimea. Using its own drones, Ukraine's Operation MoLoChKa (which roughly translates as "Moscow will fall through Crimea") has struck around 200 Russian vessels, bringing traffic in the strategic Sea of Azov to a virtual standstill. Ukrainians bristle at the suggestion that Russia and Ukraine are playing the same game. Kyiv is attempting to loosen Moscow's grip on occupied territory, they point out, while Russia is preventing Ukraine from exporting badly needed grain to the international market. With Ukraine's summer grain harvest well under way, this is all happening at the worst possible time. "It's the most sensitive period," says Volodymyr Slavinskyi, trading director for Nibulon, one of the country's leading grain exporters. "Farmers need to quickly harvest grains from the fields, not to lose the crop. They need to be able to sell the crop they harvested and reinvest money in the next production cycle." The impact of a prolonged shutdown of Ukraine's ports are likely to be severe. Ukraine is one of the world's largest producers of grain and oilseeds, supplying around 6% of global wheat exports before Russia's full-scale invasion and 10% of corn exports. But reports suggest, external its export capacity has dropped by at least a third since Russia launched its full-scale invasion. The Black Sea remains a vital export route for the country. Last year, the Greater Odesa ports accounted for more than 73 million tonnes of Ukraine's maritime exports, with grain accounting for 38 million tonnes. With almost no vessels currently moving on Ukraine's Black Sea shipping corridor, traders are already counting the cost of this summer's closure. "I would say we've already lost the ability to deliver to global customers around half a million or 700,000 metric tons of Ukrainian grains and oilseeds," Slavinskyi says. Away from the port, Odesa is determined to show off a very different side. The summer season is in full swing. The beaches are packed as visitors descend on the Black Sea from all over Ukraine. Buskers perform on the city's famous Potemkin Stairs, while sunbathers barely flinch as the sirens sound and explosions rumble in the distance. In a video published on Monday, swimmers were seen removing a Russian drone from the water as holidaymakers look on. They know the risks. In late June, 26-year-old Daria Kravchenko was killed when shrapnel from an intercepted Russian drone landed on the beach. This week, holidaymakers on Russia's equally Black Sea coast suffered a similar fate when an intercepted Ukrainian drone crashed onto a busy beach. Local authorities said seven people were killed, including three children. It's not clear what Ukraine was targeting, but this war on ships and ports has many casual victims. Sailors, dockworkers or people simply unlucky enough to live or work nearby. Outside Odesa, after a recent drone explosion, we found 83-year-old Andrii Dudik, surveying the mangled wreckage of his house and garden. He was physically unscathed and remarkably sanguine about the drone that had shattered his routine afternoon nap just hours earlier. "I was lying there, wondering what I was going to do this afternoon. Now I know," he joked. Did he feel like an accidental victim of Russia's attacks on the nearby ports, I asked him. "Absolutely," he replied. "And I won't forget it." Additional reporting by Kristina Volk, Anastasiia Levchenko, Volodymyr Lozhko and Joshua Cheetham

item.title: Banned from football at home, Afghan women's team reunite 8,000 miles away
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8dnrpmgv4yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Banned from football at home, Afghan women's team reunite 8,000 miles away - Published The changing room is busy with footballers going through their pre-match routines. Some stretch and tighten their boots, others embrace. "Be strong as always because we are representing Afghan women," says midfielder Fatima Haidari to fellow members of Afghan Women United. Applause erupts in the room where an Afghan flag hangs and a patriotic song is played. As the women sing along some struggle to hold back tears. There's a final team huddle with words of encouragement from their coach before they head out to the pitch – a place that for years they had been told they did not belong. The 23-player squad, selected from Afghan players now living abroad, has travelled to New Zealand for a training camp and to play two unofficial friendly games against the Cook Islands. This is the first time they have been together since football governing body Fifa ruled in April that they could represent their country in official matches in the future. Previously, they would have needed the approval of the Afghanistan Football Federation. This was not possible under the Taliban, who returned to power in August 2021, imposing wide-ranging restrictions on women and girls, including barring them from secondary school and university, most professions and organised sport. The country's national women's team, formed in 2007, could no longer play and its members were among those evacuated and resettled in countries including Australia, the UK and Portugal. Years of campaigning led to the creation of a refugee team, which became Afghan Women United. Thanks to Fifa's ruling, it can now try to qualify for international competitions such as the Olympics and World Cup. Gathered in New Zealand, the squad is excited to be playing together - as asylum seekers living in various countries it has been hard for them to get the travel documents in order to train as a team over the past five years. Sitting in the hotel in Auckland the day before the match, Manozh Noori, who has short hair, wears a T-shirt and knee-length shorts - a look that she says has often drawn criticism from relatives for looking too masculine. As the 23-year-old speaks to BBC Global Women about her family, her voice begins to falter. She pauses, takes a deep breath and looks away for a moment before continuing. There are no tears, but the emotion is clear. Noori now lives in Australia but she grew up playing football with boys in the streets of Kabul. After seeing women's football on television, she secretly joined local clubs and gradually rose through the ranks in Afghanistan. She knew her older brother would disapprove so she tried to reduce the risk of being recognised by wearing a face covering. Over six years, she won league titles, national championships and individual awards. Eventually her success became impossible to hide. In about 2018 her fellow players persuaded her to remove her face covering for a TV interview, which was shown on the news along with highlights of their match. Then she had to face the reality that her brother might see it. "I was so scared," she recalls. "I kept thinking, 'He's going to see me. He's going to know.'" In desperation, she tried to stop the family from watching the news by turning off the electricity, but word soon reached her brother and he was furious, she says. "He was screaming," Noori says. "'You told us you were studying. You said you wanted to become a teacher or a doctor. What is this?'" He threatened to cut his ties with the family if she didn't stop, she adds. "My mother was crying. She told me, 'He's the person who supports us financially. How are we going to survive?'" Noori did stop playing for a while, but eventually started again. She says her other brother, who lives in Germany, sent money to help finance her dream. When the Taliban took over in 2021, Noori decided to flee, but first she buried her football medals and trophies in the garden of her family home. More than four years later, they remain there. "One day I will go back and dig them out," she says, briefly smiling at the thought. "Football helped me get my mum and sister out of Afghanistan," she says. Two years after she moved to Australia and established herself as a football player, she was able to bring them over as well. This meant her sister was able to study again - even though her brother didn't want them playing sports, he always supported their education. "I hope my brother now realises I am not a bad person," says Noori. Afghan Reunited: The fight for football BBC Global Women follows Afghan female footballers as they return to the pitch As she and the team prepare for the matches in Auckland, many of them describe football as the reason they survived one of the most turbulent periods in their country's recent history. "If I wasn't a footballer, I would still be in Afghanistan, one of millions of girls who are not allowed to study, speak up or choose their own future," says Mursal Sadat, who also lives in Australia. Now 24, she works as a football coach, youth facilitator and advocate for refugees, women's rights and human rights. In Afghanistan, she says she was often judged, harassed and told that no-one would want to marry a woman who played sport. Today she is engaged to a man who is still in Afghanistan, and says he and his family are supportive of her work and place on the national team. "They tell me, 'You are the pride of our family. We are so lucky to have you.'" As the players step out into the driving Auckland rain to face the Cook Islands, they channel their energy and determination, unfazed by the weather. They have faced much tougher conditions back home. As a teenager, defender Najma Arefi trained in temperatures above 45C (113F) because girls were often given the least desirable training slots. Still, she persisted. The 22-year-old's efforts eventually helped a Herat-based team win a national championship. The victory, she says, changed attitudes towards women's sport in the city. "There were billboards of us across Herat," she recalls. "People were proud. More families started letting their daughters play football." She now lives in Doncaster in northern England. She arrived in the UK after the Taliban takeover. She describes herself as an extrovert and says she now has opportunities she never imagined growing up in Afghanistan. She studies criminal justice at college, plays football and makes decisions independently. "Having that freedom is incredible," she says. Yet she admits she often feels guilty and desperately sad about the freedoms denied to women back home. "Millions of girls don't have the chance to study or follow their dreams. I feel I have to make the most of every opportunity. "Sometimes I put too much pressure on myself," she says, tears rolling down her face. She thanks Khalida Popal, who founded the original Afghan women's team, for pushing Fifa to recognise them now they are in exile. "To receive Fifa's recognition without the approval of the Taliban" has made history, she says. This official status is "something I'll always be proud of", she says. When the BBC asked the Taliban's director for sports, Ahmadullah Wasiq, about Fifa backing the women's team, he declined to comment. But he said he would like Fifa to visit the country and resume its support for football there in general - the organisation largely withdrew after the Taliban came to power. Fifa has previously said any resumption of support would depend on women being allowed to play. The game in Auckland turns out to be unforgiving. A single goal in the first match hands the Cook Islands a 1-0 victory. Three days later, despite the Afghan team's best efforts, the Cook Islands win again, this time 3-0. Yet for the players, these matches represent something far more significant than two defeats. A return to the pitch and proof that despite exile, separation from their families and years of uncertainty, Afghanistan's women footballers refused to disappear. - This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

item.title: El-Sayed's victory sends tremors through Democratic Party
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp309ng0xq1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
El-Sayed's victory sends tremors through Democratic Party - Published The tremors from Abdul El-Sayed's victory in Michigan's Senate primary will have been felt hundreds of miles away by the Democratic Party leadership. In a year in which Republicans appear to be facing significant electoral headwinds, Democratic primary voters have taken a chance on a left-wing insurgent, raising the stakes in a Senate race in November that could decide overall control of the upper chamber. The question is whether the way El-Sayed has electrified the party base and tapped into their anger will work on general election voters. And whether an unabashedly left-wing Democrat can win in a swing state. The party establishment, which had backed his opponent, will hope so. Primary results across five states on Tuesday were a snapshot of the mood of the American electorate three months before the midterm elections. Here are four key takeaways from the results. 1) A new left-wing warrior Abdul El-Sayed's victory on Tuesday night in Michigan's contentious Democratic primary race for Senate was hardly a surprise. He had led by a comfortable margin over congresswoman Haley Stevens for weeks. While the final projected result was much closer than those surveys had suggested, again raising questions about modern polling accuracy, it doesn't diminish the shockwaves the victory of the former Michigan health official is sending throughout the Democratic Party. El-Sayed, the child of Egyptian immigrants, ran on a left-wing platform with the backing of such liberal stalwarts as Senators Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. - Left-wing political outsider wins Democratic Senate primary in Michigan - Published2 days ago Stevens had the backing of Democratic leadership in Washington, an established record as an elected official in Michigan and deep financial pockets, including $32m from Aipac - the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. Outside groups favoured her over El-Sayed by a margin of nine-to-one. None of it mattered. In debates and on the stump, El-Sayed proved to be the more gifted candidate, and Democrats seemed open to his policies, including government-sponsored health insurance, efforts to lower drug costs, higher taxes on the wealthy and campaign finance reform. His campaign refrain - "money out of politics, money in your pocket" - has been a common one among left-wing candidates this election cycle. This sets up a general election contest against former Republican congressman Mike Rogers, who ran unopposed. It will provide perhaps the most dramatic, high-stakes test of whether a left-wing candidate can win a general election race in a true battleground state. Given the narrowness of El-Sayed's primary victory, he has considerable work ahead if he wants to unite the party before November's vote. While El-Sayed did well with higher-educated liberals, he'll need to win over the lower-income voters who backed Stevens in Detroit and in more rural areas. These are voters whose preferences the pre-election polling did not seem to adequately reflect. If El-Sayed loses to Rogers, it would be a major blow to Democratic hopes of retaking control of the US Senate given a Republican hasn't won a Senate race in the state since 1994. If he wins, however, it could provide left-wing Democrats with proof of concept for why a left-wing candidate for president in 2028 could be more successful than the kind of establishment centrists the party has nominated in recent contests. And with Michigan's position as a key early state on the Democratic presidential primary calendar, the state will have an outsized say in who the party's nominee will be. 2) Some pro-Israel Democrats had a bad night Stevens was the highest-profile Aipac-backed candidate to lose on Tuesday night. In lesser-watched races, the results were more mixed. Elsewhere in Michigan, Democratic Socialist Donavan McKinney beat incumbent Shri Thanedar, who has been an outspoken supporter of continued US support for Israel. He became the latest party House incumbent to be ousted in the primaries. William Lawrence, who has called for an immediate end to US arms sales to Israel, defeated two centrist Democrats in a House of Representatives district in Michigan that is likely to be a key electoral battleground in November. If the mood of the Democratic voters has soured on pro-Israel politicians in Michigan, and in previous races in New York and Colorado, that was not the case in the Missouri and Washington results. In Washington, congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who supports military aid for Israel, easily turned away a left-wing challenger. She is one of the few Democratic incumbents in districts Trump won in 2024 - and will be a prime target for Republicans in November. Meanwhile, in a solidly liberal Missouri district, Wesley Bell denied a comeback bid from Cori Bush, a founding member of the "squad" of left-wing congresswomen. Two years ago, he unseated her in part because of her criticism of Israel. 3) Voters reject Republican measures in the Midwest While most of the contests on Tuesday night were intraparty primary fights, there were a couple of notable votes that could provide evidence that the overall mood of the electoral continues to tilt toward the Democrats. In Missouri, voters overwhelmingly rejected a ballot measure that would have made citizen-backed amendments to the state constitution more difficult to enact. In recent years, such citizen-driven efforts have been used to push Democratic initiatives that had no chance of passage in the Republican-controlled state legislature. They include protecting abortion rights and raising the minimum wage. Meanwhile in Kansas, voters rejected a ballot measure that would have have required the state's supreme court justices to stand for election. At the moment, they are appointed by the governor and a commission of lawyers. In 2024, the state high court had ruled that the right to abortion was protected by the Kansas constitution - a decision Republicans said was out-of-step with the will of state voters. Both efforts were pushed by state Republicans and, in both cases, the proposals were easily defeated. 4) Trump's endorsement still (mostly) matters It was largely a good night for Trump-backed Republicans, who earned a few victories in their primaries. John James won Michigan's Republican nomination for governor despite being heavily outspent by his wealthy opponent. Trump not only endorsed James but appeared on stage with him last week. In Kansas, Republicans opted for the Trump favourite for governor amidst a crowded field. And in the Washington state race to replace outgoing Republican congressman Dan Newhouse, Amanda McKinney, the president's pick, also finished first. The 71-year-old Newhouse, who is retiring, was notable for being one of the last two remaining House Republicans to have voted to impeach Trump after the 6 January 2021 riot at the US Capitol. Given that this is a reliably conservative district, McKinney is a favourite to defeat her Democratic opponent in November, which would likely move House Republicans further to the right. It's the latest bit of evidence that old-line establishment Republicans like Newhouse are a vanishing breed. But Trump didn't get it all his own way. In Michigan, Thomas Smith defeated Trump-endorsed Amir Hassan, a former law-enforcement officer who also appeared on stage with the president, despite Smith having dropped out of the race last month while remaining on the ballot. item.title: 'My grandmother subjected my baby to female genital mutilation behind my back'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3r0vp7n0pro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'My grandmother subjected my baby to female genital mutilation behind my back' - Published Warning: This story contains descriptions of the practices involved in female genital mutilation In what activists are calling a milestone, Colombia last week became the first country in Latin America where female genital mutilation (FGM) is now illegal. As José Carlos Cueto reports, while the bill was passed unanimously in Colombia's Congress, it follows a long battle to eradicate the dangerous and often secretive procedure. Carla Quiñonez's daughter was just six months old when the baby's great-grandmother subjected her to female genital mutilation (FGM). Quiñonez (not her real name) says when her grandmother returned the baby to her, she had a fever and was swollen and bleeding. She cried constantly. "I confronted my grandmother, but she said it was normal and that I could not tell anyone." The nearest health centre was a long journey away, so Quiñonez's mother, a midwife, tried to ease the baby's pain with medicinal plants. She also challenged Quiñonez's grandmother. But the older woman would not listen. "She said that men make fun of women who have a clitoris." FGM in Colombia FGM involves the partial or total removal of the external female genitalia, as well as other injuries inflicted on those organs for non-medical reasons. It can cause medical complications, including haemorrhaging and infection, as well as complications later in life with periods and during childbirth. It can also make it difficult for a woman to experience sexual pleasure. The World Health Organization says that around the world more than 230 million girls and women alive today have been cut, predominantly in Africa. Quiñonez, 30, has been campaigning to eradicate the practice in Colombia - where it is still practised by members of her Emberá Indigenous community. Along with fellow activists and members of Colombia's Congress, she played a key role in the campaign which led to the ban. She says it was only as she grew up that she realised what was secretly happening within her community. "I always wondered why more girls than boys seemed to die shortly after birth. "I remember a young cousin of mine whose birth was attended by my mother. She was born healthy, but died three days later. "I asked my mother about it, and she told me the baby had died from 'jai', an ancestral illness." Quiñonez now believes that girls who supposedly died from "jai" actually died from complications related to FGM. A paediatrician's perspective Between 2020 and June 2026, 240 cases of FGM were recorded in Colombia. In the vast majority of instances, the girls were younger than six years old. But paediatrician Diana Ramos Mosquera says she believes this is just "the tip of the iceberg". Working at San Jorge University Hospital in Pereira, a city in Colombia's north-west coffee-growing region, she says she's seen signs of scarring, burning and mutilation when examining girls who have come in with other medical conditions. She recalls one girl who arrived with her vaginal opening sealed shut, meaning she probably would not have been able to menstruate or have sexual intercourse when she reached adulthood. "She had to undergo reconstructive surgery," Dr Ramos says. She regards FGM as a form of sexual and gender-based violence with lifelong consequences, but says this must be addressed through education, and not just punishment. "Some members of these communities genuinely believe they are doing no harm," she says. 'Culture does not kill' With around 300,000 members, the Great Emberá Nation is one of Colombia's largest Indigenous communities, with populations also living in Ecuador and Panama. One theory about why members of the community practise FGM, when it's rarely seen elsewhere in Latin America, is that the practice arrived with enslaved people from African countries. This could help explain its prevalence in Risaralda, Chocó and Valle del Cauca, neighbouring departments that either are home to, or border, large Afro-Colombian populations. Another theory is that the birth of an intersex child, hundreds of years ago, left the community with a fear of the clitoris - with many older women believing that it will grow into a penis if not cut. Others think that it stems from the patriarchal belief that a woman with an organ associated with sexual pleasure is more likely to be promiscuous. Whatever its origin, Juliana Domico, the legal representative and chief Indigenous councillor to the National Confederation of the Peoples of the Great Emberá Nation of Colombia, rejects the idea that the practice is cultural. "Our culture is our clothing, our crafts, our dances and our language, not a practice that kills. Culture does not kill." She says the new law follows years of advocacy work within the community: "We hope the law is translated into public policy, with sufficient resources to implement it." Threats and hostility Quiñonez is one of those who have advocated for change, but says she has received threats because of this - especially from men. While, traditionally, men are not meant to know about the ritual, conversations about abolishing the practice often only take place with male leaders because many Emberá women speak an indigenous language - also called Emberá - and have not necessarily learned Spanish. This can also prevent women from accessing help from doctors for their babies, a problem which Quiñonez says is compounded when they're faced by sometimes ill-informed and judgmental health staff. She says when she took her daughter to hospital with a fever caused by a urinary tract infection, the nurse berated her for "being a savage" and told her that she had got what she deserved. "I was even threatened with having my daughter taken away and placed in the care of the child welfare authorities. "Since then, I prefer not to take my daughter to hospital. I treat her with medicinal plants and medication. I never leave her side." 'Conversation cannot be avoided' Quiñonez says that there is change under way within the Emberá community, with women now discussing among themselves whether FGM should happen. She says she was moved when one grandmother reflected on carrying out FGM on her granddaughters. "She said she had never acted out of malice and had only wanted to prevent men from criticising her granddaughters." Having conversations about a different way of life can be painful, she says. "Women who have grown up without a clitoris cannot imagine a different body." It will also be difficult to speak to her own daughter about it, one day in the future, "but it is a conversation that cannot be avoided," she says. "All of us deserve to understand our bodies and to talk about them without shame." Moment earthquake shakes hospital operating room in Japan Newly-released security camera footage shows the moment last month's magnitude 6.8 quake shook Kumamoto General Hospital in Japan. Four surgeries were under way at the time. Footage from a camera in an operating room where an abdominal surgery was being performed shows medical staff shielding the patient with their bodies as equipment swayed violently, and a nurse opening a door to secure an evacuation route. According to the hospital, all four operations were successfully completed. Kumamoto General Hospital resumed normal outpatient services on 5 August , after suspending them following the earthquake on 28 July. 【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c89n8940vq8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Watch: Nasa astronauts conduct 6.5-hour spacewalk outside ISS Nasa astronauts Anil Menon and Jessica Meir ventured outside the International Space Station for a spacewalk on Thursday to install mounting hardware. The hardware will prepare the station’s 3B power channel for the future installation of new roll-out solar arrays. The spacewalk lasted 6.5 hours. item.title: Why was Taiwan’s president evacuated in the middle of the night?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cly83vm923go?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Why was Taiwan’s president evacuated in the middle of the night? President William Lai took part in an emergency evacuation drill as part of Taiwan's annual Han Kuang military exercises that are running from August 5th to 14th. The BBC’s Katy Watson explains what happened and why Taiwan is using the drills to prepare for a potential Chinese invasion. item.title: Where is Jackie? Beloved live cam eagle in critical condition
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c2el1dz7ge9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Where is Jackie? Beloved live cam eagle in critical condition Jackie, the bald eagle who has gained worldwide fame over the years, has been diagnosed with anaemia and is in "critical" condition. Jackie and her partner, Shadow, have been watched by millions of people over the years through the Big Bear Eagle Nest Cam, run by the nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley in California. The eagle is under veterinary care at the Ojai Raptor Center, and despite showing signs of improvement in her anaemia last week, her packed cell volume has dropped to 13%, down from 17%.
